body: Parked on a double yellow outside a primary school at a quarter past three, engine running, a woman waits, because the alternative is the car park and the car park is a war. Her eleven-year-old will be out in four minutes and will get straight into an argument with the seven-year-old. She goes through the presets. The first is talking about house prices. The second is playing something with a chorus she does not want either of them repeating. The third is a Christian station, and it is fine, and it is also pitched at somebody who has been in church every Sunday of their life, which she has not been for a long time and neither of her children ever has. She turns the radio off and sits in the quiet, and then the doors open.

That is where a station starts. Not with a genre and not with a gap in the market, but with a person somebody can describe in one sentence, and a description of what they are carrying around at a quarter past three.

The order here is fixed: a need, then a remit, then a number, then the catalogue, and only then a sign-on. The number is reserved at the beginning, when the station is still only a need with a remit attached.

A remit is not a genre and the difference is the whole of it. A genre says what the music sounds like. A remit says who the station is for, who is hosting it, and — this is the load-bearing clause — what it will not do. The prohibitions are what make a remit usable, because they are the only part of it that will still be doing work in two years, when there is a good song available that would grow the audience and does not belong. Anyone can honour a description of the thing they wanted to make anyway. A remit is what you consult when you want to make something else.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and holds 121 numbers, of which 46 are on air. Which is to say that most of the numbers on this dial are already spoken for by stations that have not signed on yet.

That is the expensive part, and it is deliberate. Holding a frequency for a station that may not exist for years means the number cannot be given to something that looks more promising this quarter. It cannot be recycled because the dial would look tidier arranged another way. A broadcaster holds a licence long before it transmits anything, and everybody understands why: the licence is the commitment, and the transmitter is merely the day the commitment becomes audible. Reserving the number first is what stops a station from being quietly redefined into whatever turned out to be easiest to fill.

The habit everywhere else runs the other way. Ship first, define later, watch what people click, and let the thing become whatever the numbers reward. It is a genuinely good method for building a shop and a catastrophic one for building anything that is supposed to say something, because a product shaped by response cannot hold a position — it can only hold whatever position was popular last month. Nobody in that loop is lying. They are simply not able to promise anything, and after a while they stop noticing that they cannot.

The host is settled at the remit stage as well, before a single track is chosen, because a station is a voice before it is ever a playlist. The wrong voice will make the right music land wrong, and no amount of catalogue afterwards will fix it. So the personas come first, each carrying a lane and a manner, and the music is then written to a station that already knows who is speaking on it.
After that it is simply catalogue, which is the unglamorous middle where most of the years go.

The obvious alternative is to build the music first and find it a home afterwards, and it deserves a fair hearing because it is how nearly every playlist in the world is assembled, it is much faster, and it never leaves a number sitting empty. But music gathered before there is a remit is music gathered to somebody’s taste, and a taste is not a person. You end up with a very good collection of tracks that share a feel and answer nobody in particular, which is why so many stations are pleasant to have on and impossible to describe. Then a slot gets found for it, and the slot moves later when a better one comes up, because nothing was ever promised about where it would live.
A number that can be moved is not an address.

A man of thirty-four is painting the small bedroom at the back of the house, badly, because there is a baby coming in seven weeks and this is the one job he said he would do himself. He has not been inside a church since he was christened in one, and has no plans to be. A friend who helped shift the furniture left a station on and neither of them turned it off. Somewhere in the second coat he notices he is singing — not loudly, and not the chorus of anything he could name — about being grateful for the house and the people in it. His wife is on the landing sorting through a box of cables and hears him and says nothing at all about it, then or later.

That man is the sentence. He is not a demographic and he is not a market segment; he is a description of a person and of what he is carrying, and a station was reserved a number and written a catalogue in order to be playable to him with the door open.

The honest cost is time, and the people who pay it are listeners. A number can sit reserved for a long while, and somebody who needs that exact station this year may find that it does not answer yet. There are more silent frequencies on this dial than live ones. Every one of them is a promise that has not come due, and a promise that has not come due is indistinguishable, from the outside, from an empty space.

Which is exactly why they are held rather than filled. A dial that could be rearranged whenever something more promising came along would be a shop shelf with numbers painted on it, and everything anybody had ever learned about where things sit would be wrong by the following spring. Holding a number costs patience now so that a link somebody shares five years from now still opens on the thing it was meant to open on. That is not administration. That is the difference between an address and a label.

So the sequence is the argument. A need somebody can state in a sentence, a remit including what it will not do, a host, a number reserved at the beginning, then years of catalogue written to fit — and when it goes live, nothing else on the dial moves. A frequency here is not where a station ended up. It is where a station was promised, before there was anything to put in it.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every one of them came off the same production line as the one described above.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 376.20 — Melody’s Sparkle. It is the station on this dial where you can hear the remit most plainly, prohibitions and all: pre-evangelistic pop about gratitude, family and everyday wonder, written to be playable to somebody who is not in church yet. Clean, warm, and never preachy — and that last clause is a refusal, not a style note. It is why the station can be on in a car at a quarter past three with two children in the back, or on a speaker in a spare bedroom with a man in it who would not describe himself as anything. Put it on where the people you actually live near can hear it, which is the case it was reserved a number to serve.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a prospectus. You are not being asked to approve of a process, and nobody needs you to find the reserving of numbers interesting. Put HM 376.20 on this week in the room where the radio actually lives, and leave it on while the ordinary business of the afternoon carries on around it. Somebody in your house who has never asked you a single question about any of this will end up singing something. That is what the number was held for.
